Photograph: Claudia Deganutti Italy Hundreds camp in Rome heatwave as Meloni government cracks down on squats Spin Time provides homes, food banks and after-school clubs but the authorities have locked out residents Angela Giuffrida in Rome Wed 5 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Hundreds of people have spent a week sleeping in tents in the Rome heat amid a standoff between Giorgia Meloni’s far-right government and local politicians over the future of Italy’s most high-profile centre for housing and social assistance. A minor fire last week forced the evacuation of the building, occupied by grassroots groups since 2013, and it has remained closed as the Meloni government attempts to crack down on such squatted properties. “It’s an awful situation, made worse by this heatwave,” said Petronela Podaro, a domestic worker from Romania camped outside the building, its huge red gates locked up, in Rome’s Esquilino district. The fire inside Spin Time Labs broke out in the early hours of 29 July in an external area and was quickly extinguished by residents before it could spread. View image in fullscreen Young people with the belongings they managed to save before the eviction. Residents are now living on the street, carrying their possessions in suitcases and bags. Photograph: Claudia Deganutti Police evacuated the 10-floor complex, citing the need for safety checks, forcing about 400 residents including children, elderly and disabled people on to the street. Spin Time Labs, an initiative supported by Rome’s leftwing council and the Vatican, has long been targeted for eviction by Meloni’s government, which regards occupied buildings as dens for criminality. The centre, which over the last decade has transformed into a space offering various social and cultural services, including a food bank, a restaurant and co-working, hit the headlines in 2019 after an aide to the late Pope Francis, Cardinal Konrad Krajewski, climbed down a manhole to restore the electricity, provoking the fury of Matteo Salvini, who was the interior minister at the time and is now deputy prime minister. Various Italian writers, actors and film directors, including the Oscar winner Paolo Sorrentino, have appealed for the residents to be allowed back in or for alternative accommodation to be provided. Roberto Saviano, an author and high-profile critic of Meloni’s government, visited the scene on Monday and described the centre as a “symbol of democracy” rather than a criminal act. View image in fullscreen Tents were provided by the civil protection department and set up on the street in front of Spin Time. Photograph: Claudia Deganutti The building is now under two judicial seizure orders – one linked to the private owner’s long-running legal battle to regain possession and the other to the fire. Although shutting down Spin Time is in its plans, the interior ministry has failed to carry out an eviction order first issued by a judge in 2020, two years before Meloni came to power, reportedly due to fears over the social and legal repercussions of forcing vulnerable people on to the street. Earlier this year, the ministry, led by Matteo Piantedosi, was ordered to pay €21m in damages for failing to act on the eviction order. As Rome’s council, which along with an army of volunteers has provided camp beds, food, drink and medical assistance, scrambles for a solution, including offering to buy the building so that the community can be maintained, Spin Time’s residents are facing more time on the street. “There are lots of children, newborns, elderly and disabled people, and those with complicated illnesses who are struggling in this heat,” said Podaro, who is unemployed. “But we are very united community, of all nationalities and backgrounds. What this government doesn’t seem to understand is that if we had a decent job and could earn money, then we wouldn’t be in this situation.” View image in fullscreen Petronela (right) and Nicoletta are neighbours, having lived on the same floor at Spin Time since 2013. They are friends and also part of the same extended family. Photograph: Claudia Deganutti Spin Time has provided a lifeline for hundreds of people, including Marco Perilli, an Italian construction worker who was one of the community’s first residents after becoming homeless following a divorce. Perilli was also among the residents who put the fire out. “There was panic but we were able to extinguish it within about 20 minutes,” he said. “Firefighters made the area safe but then the police arrived and, because we were afraid, we all went outside. They locked the gates and told us we couldn’t go back inside due to the safety checks. Within a few hours, the building was seized.” Perilli said police searched the building for drugs and weapons. “It backfired because they found nothing,” he added, while claiming “the fire was exploited as an excuse for eviction”. “But we will continue to fight against it,” he said. “The Meloni government needs to think carefully about the real meaning of power. Power is not about attacking poor people – this government is at war against the poor.” Benjamin Macshane, a British volunteer cook in Spin Time’s restaurant, said the initiative provided more than just shelter. “There’s co-working, there’s an after-school club, there’s migration assistance, a food bank, a barbers, an auditorium … I can’t think of anywhere else in the world that has so many different avenues for a community to grow.” Explore more on these topics Italy Giorgia Meloni Europe news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

REUTERS/Manuel Ausloos/File Photo By Leigh Thomas PARIS, Sept 8 (Reuters) - Teenagers more accustomed to smartphones than Shakespeare are reading at the worst levels seen this century, driving a broader decline in education, a global student ‌assessment found. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development's 2025 test of 760,000 15-year-olds across 91 countries ‌showed reading, mathematics and science scores at their lowest levels since data began to be collected in 2000. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement On average, students were reading at ​a level that had in the past been expected of students one year younger, according to the OECD's latest Programme for International Student Assessment released on Tuesday. A 2012 reading high of 501 on PISA's index had declined to a score of 466 last year. The test is widely regarded as the world's leading gauge of educational performance ‌and its results are closely scrutinised by ⁠governments and educators. "In reading, more screen time and less reading for pleasure have gone hand in hand with weaker results," OECD head Mathias Cormann told a press conference. "We're ⁠also seeing more hasty reading, students rushing through a text and giving a quick wrong answer." Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Reading scores fell more sharply in students from better-off backgrounds, the study added. Hindered by falling reading standards, average teenage science and maths skills were also ​at their ​lowest this century. Science fell from a 2009 high ​of 506 on the index to 486, while ‌maths was down from 502 to 469 in the same period. East Asia was the best-performing region. Chinese cities that participated in the test, Japan, Korea, Singapore and Taiwan had the best educational systems with Britain and Estonia the only countries outside the region that made it into the top 10 in reading, mathematics and science. DIGITAL DISTRACTION Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement The report stopped short of endorsing smartphone bans in schools. But it said that digital distraction is linked to ‌lower science scores in 59 of 82 education systems studied ​and more than one in four students say devices distract classmates ​in science lessons. The OECD said students reported spending ​3.4 hours per weekday for leisure on digital devices on average in OECD member ‌countries and another 3 hours per weekday in ​the classroom and at home ​for learning purposes. Digital devices could be used to improve learning, but only up to a point, Cormann said. If used more than five hours a day, results started to fall, he added. The study ​also found that nearly half of students ‌use artificial intelligence chatbots regularly for learning, but those who use them for drafting essays, ​summarizing texts and researching topics generally score about 20 points lower in science, equivalent to a ​year's learning.
